 Mike Crisolago Sat, October 24, 2026 at 11:00 AM EDT 6 min read richlifeshawtydred/Instagram In June 2021, Atlanta influencer Shawty Dred — known for flaunting mansions, money and luxury cars on social media — was asked in an interview where he saw himself in five years. 
 His answer: "Having $100 million in my bank account." 
 Five years on, Shawty Dred — real name Mercedes Reshard New — has been indicted in the Northern District of Georgia for allegedly stealing $4 million via SNAP fraud.

 "Mr. 'Shawty Dred' allegedly stole food assistance benefits in Georgia from the poorest Americans," USDA Inspector General John Walk said in a statement accompanying the indictment announcement. "He then flaunted his luxurious living off fraudulent proceeds on Instagram and TikTok." 
 SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program) fraud is, unfortunately, not uncommon, with a January USDA Inspector General report predicting $233 million in fraud losses for 2026. 
 But New's alleged fraud spanned six years, leaving questions unanswered about both the duration and the wide scope of the operation — which allegedly included 350 different fake SNAP accounts. 
 'Literally stole food out of children's mouths' 
 Authorities in New's case said his alleged 350 fake SNAP accounts "were created using stolen identities." They also alleged that New had SNAP EBT cards — which recipients swipe at retailers to use their benefits — sent to addresses around Atlanta and that he even became a licensed SNAP retailer himself. 
 And despite allegedly stealing $660,000 in SNAP benefits, getting arrested for selling SNAP benefits, being found in possession of 14 EBT cards and having his SNAP store shut down in 2025, the statement says New still managed to get multiple new EBT cards mailed out to him. 
 All told, he "allegedly duped" the Georgia Department of Human Services (DHS) Division of Family & Children Services into giving him around $4.6 million in SNAP benefits through "fraudulently established beneficiary accounts" — from which authorities claim he pocketed $4 million. Authorities arrested him on Oct. 13. 
 When asked how New allegedly continued to get away with the fraud, a Georgia DHS spokesperson told Moneywise that they "cannot comment on open investigations or prosecutions," but that "DHS continuously works on fraud prevention methodologies, including customer education, enhanced card security features, and more aggressive investigation capabilities in an effort to protect the integrity of the program and our customers' benefits." 
 Story Continues Meanwhile, the indictment statement says New "flaunted his extravagant lifestyle" to his millions of social media followers, "flying on private jets, posing with ultra-luxury Rolls-Royce and Maybach vehicles [and] handling massive stacks of cash." 
 With news of the indictment, social media users took to his Instagram account to air their anger. 
 "$4.6 million of our tax dollars though? Literally stole food out of children's mouths. Shame on you and all involved," one commenter wrote on a video of New flaunting a Rolls Royce and mansion. On another video with New holding a stack of cash, a person wrote, "Wow you're so rich! Look at all of those tax payer dollars you're holding!"

 How to protect your SNAP benefits 
 With most EBT cards not chip-enabled to protect against skimming of their data from theft devices secretly placed in payment terminals, organized crime rings can steal people's benefits without them realizing it — until they go to pay for their food and they have a $0 balance. The federal government, meanwhile, no longer replaces stolen SNAP money. 
 The USDA Inspector General's Office told Moneywise that they just released a SNAP fraud alert , which warns that theft "is occurring nationwide" and offers the following tips to reduce your risk of falling victim: 
 Lock your EBT card when it's not in use. 
 Protect and regularly change your pin number — including before receiving new benefits. 
 Remain wary of damaged or tampered card readers. 
 Be vigilant about cameras that could spot and steal your pin number or card information. 
 Georgia's DHS also advised to "practice good online security habits" and regularly check your EBT balance for unusual activity. They added that those who do suspect fraudulent activity on their account should "change their PIN and lock or replace their card immediately and then quickly report the incident to the DHS Office of Inspector General." 
 The USDA estimates that an average of 42.1 million people accessed SNAP benefits each month in 2025, costing the government $101.7 billion. 
 Priya Fielding-Singh, a food policy expert with George Washington University's Global Food Institute, previously told Moneywise that SNAP fraud requires low-income families that rely on that money "to take on debt, defer paying other expenses or reduce how much they are eating to make their money stretch further that month." 
 Massive SNAP cuts from the Trump-endorsed One Big Beautiful Bill also threaten to push millions of the neediest Americans — including children — out of the program. The shift of 75% of SNAP funding being shouldered by states also means that there's less money at local levels to root out fraud. 
 "It will increase the budgetary pressure and will make it more difficult for states to allocate funds to benefit card theft prevention," the Government Accountability Office's Kathryn Larin recently told Oregon Public Broadcasting.
